name: Esther Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'll be honest, though I'm not sure I know enough about AI to say much clever.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a private agency in a well-off suburb, where the families pay themselves rather than the council. So the visits are longer, an hour or two, and a lot of it is company as well as care: helping Mrs Whitfield shower, then doing her crossword with her, then making lunch. I drive about six clients a day in the agency's small car. I'm still quite new, I left school early and only got into care two years ago after working in a bakery, and I'm still learning things like stoma care. The families can be demanding, they text the office if I'm five minutes late, and that wears me out more than the work does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That sounds sensible, to be honest. People always say the next big thing is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and leave it there. With friends after church I'd say it's good, people want people. I hardly post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means we can keep to our plan. Daniel, my husband, is in the last year of his electrician apprenticeship, and we want to try for our first baby once he's qualified. The trouble is the agency only pays the basic maternity pay, so we're saving to cover it, and we've got about three months put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep saving, and finish my care certificate so I can ask for a small raise before the baby. I've started using a chat app now and then to plan cheap meals for the week, which my sister showed me, and I'd keep doing that. We'd stop eating out and put that money toward the baby fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. A bit nervous about the money for when I'm off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long would you want to be off with a baby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A year, at least. My mum stayed home with us and I'd like to do the same for a while. On basic maternity pay, a year off means the savings have to cover nearly everything, so we're counting every pound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the families can be demanding. Does that ever make you think about leaving?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes. One son texted the office because I'd folded his mother's towels wrong. But they pay well for the hours, better than the council agencies, so I'd stay.

say: I'm **not surprised**, and people want people.
I'd tell friends after church it's **good news** and hardly post anything.
think: We can keep to our plan of a **first baby** once my husband qualifies.
The agency pays only **basic maternity pay**, so our savings must cover it.
do: Finish the **care certificate** and ask for a small raise before the baby.
Stop **eating out** and put the money in the baby fund.
Keep using a **chat app** now and then to plan cheap meals.
feel: **Settled**, but nervous about money while she's **off work**.
S0.quote: On basic maternity pay, a year off means the savings have to cover nearly everything, so we're counting every pound.
fieldNote: Her plans centre on a **first baby** and a year at home, like her mother.
Money pressure comes from **basic maternity pay**, not technology.
Uses AI lightly for **meal planning**, picked up from her sister.

steps.text: Finish the care certificate and ask for a raise
Move eating-out money into the baby fund
Plan to try for a first baby once her husband qualifies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office jobs change, and hands-on later. I'd mostly be fine then, wouldn't I?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good for anyone who uses it well, but care is still about trust. I'd say families should check on their parents themselves more, not just through an app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the families I work for would be the first to buy fancy gadgets, sensors and smart cameras and the like. They like the newest things. My job would stay, but I'd be watched more, every minute logged, and they'd text the office even more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever the agency brings in, once I've seen the others manage it. I'd keep saving for the baby and finish the certificate. I'd ask the manager if there's a senior carer path, because I'd like to be the one who trains new girls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about losing the job, about being watched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be watched more. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A camera in an old woman's kitchen that her son checks from his office would feel like the families don't trust me. A sensor that says I was in the bathroom eight minutes, not ten. It's not wrong, I suppose, but it would sting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Daniel's work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Electricians would be busy, I think, wiring all these sensors in. Daniel's actually pleased about it. So in our house, this one might even be good.

think: Wealthy families would buy **sensors and cameras** first, because they like new things.

do: Learn the agency's **new tools** once others manage them.

feel: **Uneasy** about being **watched**, not about losing work.

fieldNote: Her worry is **surveillance** by wealthy families, not job loss.

Steady with tech: she'll learn tools **after colleagues** do.

steps.text: Learn the agency's new monitoring tools once colleagues have

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots by 2031. My families would buy them the first year they could, I know they would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sad, old people need a real person. At church I'd say families should take their parents in, like it used to be. I wouldn't make a fuss online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the private families go first. They've got the money, they like new things, and a robot doesn't get the towels wrong. So by 2031 or 2032 I think my job is gone, and I'd likely have a baby by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the baby forward a little, so I've had my year off before the robots come. I'd save harder, from three months toward six, and ask Daniel to take on extra jobs while electricians are busy wiring things. Once the baby's older, I'd look at care home work, where councils pay and change might come slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be thinking about the baby and the money at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bring the baby forward. Isn't that a risk, with all this coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But waiting doesn't make it safer, the robots come either way. I'd rather have my year at home with the baby while I still have a job to come back to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Daniel's job feel safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than mine for a while. Someone has to install all of it. After 2031, I don't know, but he's practical and he'd find something.

Families should **take their parents in**, like it used to be.
think: **Private families** would buy robots first, because they can afford them.
My job could be **gone** by 2031 or 2032, probably with a baby at home.

feel: **Anxious**, juggling the **baby** and the money in her mind.

fieldNote: Her clients' **wealth** makes her job more exposed, not less.

Her husband's **electrician** trade gives the household a few safer years.

steps.text: Try for a first baby a year earlier than planned

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots around 2034. A little more time to have a family first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time for families to plan, and for young people to learn something steady. I'd not say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it suits our plans. I'd have the baby, take my year, and come back for a few years before the robots. By 2034 I might want to be home more anyway with two little ones, and Daniel would be fully qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep to our plan: Daniel qualifies, we try for the baby, I finish my certificate. I'd learn the agency's tools once they're common. I'd keep three months saved and maybe look at a senior carer job when I'm back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might want to be home more anyway. Would one income be enough?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Daniel's busy. We'd live small, which we already do. I'd rather live small than have both of us working and a stranger raising the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older carers who've done this twenty years and have nothing else. And my clients, the lonely ones. A robot won't do the crossword with Mrs Whitfield.

I'd keep my comments **short and simple**.

steps.text: Try for a first baby after her husband qualifies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots around 2039. My children would be at school by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people are sensible. I'd tell my younger cousins to learn a trade, like Daniel did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's the gentlest one for us. I'd have years of care work and a family by 2039. The end is still the same, though, and I'd be nearly 40 looking for something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my certificate, then the senior carer course in a couple of years. We'd have a baby as planned. I'd start using AI more once it's normal, and maybe save for a small house by 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A little uneasy about what I'd do at 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What might you do at 40?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know yet. Maybe help at the children's school, or something at church that pays a bit. I'd have ten years to work it out, which is a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the extra time make you see the job differently now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'd stop worrying so much about the son who texts about the towels. The job is not forever, so I'd enjoy the crosswords with my clients more.

I'd tell younger cousins to **learn a trade**, like my husband did.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the families I work for would buy robots straight away, and I'd likely have a baby and no job to go back to. What would help is decent maternity pay in care, and help for families who want to look after their own parents at home instead.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the families who pay. Everyone talks about the carers. The rich families decide this, and they'll pick whatever is newest.

headlineQuote: The rich families decide this, and they'll pick whatever is newest.
portrait: A 27-year-old care worker at a **private agency** in a well-off suburb, doing long companionship visits.
Married to an **apprentice electrician**; planning a first baby and a year at home.
Traditional and thrifty; uses AI **now and then** for meal planning.
Sees **wealthy clients** as the first to buy sensors and robots.
Most anxious in **AGI by 2028**, when robots might arrive with a baby at home.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, as rich clients buy robots while she's on maternity leave.
whatWouldHelp: Help for **families caring** for parents at home.
